# Acknowledgements {#sec-98-acknowledgements}

This book has a long prehistory. Earlier versions were written between 2018
and 2024 under the title *Tidy Portfoliomanagement in R*, and substantial
parts of the present material began there, in a different voice and a
different structure. The people who wrote with me then are the reason the
present text could be built as fast as it was.

**Elizabet Sanyal** wrote the first working versions of the covariance,
expected-return and fully flexible views material, and her critique of the
backtesting chapter shaped how this edition separates demonstration from
diagnosis. **Dominik Brändle** contributed the original backtesting and
optimization code. **Lukas Salcher** and **Merlin Bartel** contributed to the
earlier chapters, and their research with me on estimation error, on the
economic value of forecast accuracy and on diversifying estimation errors
underlies Parts III and VIII.

The developers of `PortfolioAnalytics` and `PerformanceAnalytics`, in
particular Brian G. Peterson and Peter Carl, have maintained the machinery this
book is about for the better part of two decades. Where a chapter records a
default that fails or a constraint that is dropped, it does so with respect for
a package whose ambition is the reason such things can be found at all, and
every finding of that kind has been reported upstream. Ross Bennett's work on
the package's second-generation interface is what the chapters call.

Christoph Scheuch, Stefan Voigt and Patrick Weiss, and Guillaume Coqueret and
Tony Guida, wrote the two books beside which this one is meant to sit. Their
example settled most of the questions about how a book of this kind should be
built, and the reader who wants the data acquisition or the machine learning
that this book cites rather than reproduces will find it in theirs.

The students of the portfolio management courses at the University of
Liechtenstein have worked through earlier versions of most exercises, and
their questions are the reason several of the callouts exist. The simulated
market was built for their course; the caveats in @sec-90-data-description are
the ones they found.

Finally, to my family, for the evenings.
